nameStory: The name 'figwort' comes from an old belief that this plant could cure fig-shaped lumps or swellings on the body. Medieval herbalists followed the 'doctrine of signatures,' thinking that plants resembled the body parts they could heal. The scientific name 'nodosa' means 'knotty,' referring to the plant's swollen stem joints.
description: Common figwort is a tall, sturdy perennial herb that can grow 3-6 feet high with a square, upright stem. It produces clusters of small, unusual reddish-brown flowers that look almost like tiny helmets or pouches. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with large, coarsely-toothed leaves arranged in pairs along the stem. Despite its humble looks, it's actually a member of the snapdragon family.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, helmet-shaped flowers in loose clusters, colored an unusual reddish-brown or maroon - they feel papery and look almost artificial, with a distinctive two-lipped opening

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Distinctly square, hollow stems that feel ridged when you run your finger along them, often with swollen joints where leaves attach

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs with coarsely-toothed edges that feel slightly rough and have a somewhat unpleasant, weedy smell when crushed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny dark seeds that rattle inside when the capsule is shaken

habitat: Look for common figwort in moist, partially shaded areas like woodland edges, disturbed ground, and waste places. It thrives in rich, damp soil and often grows near old foundations, along streams, or in areas where the ground has been cultivated or disturbed. You might find it mixed with other weedy plants in semi-wild spaces.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground with fresh green, opposite leaves appearing along the distinctive square stems.
seasonality.summer: The characteristic reddish-brown helmet flowers bloom from mid to late summer, attracting wasps and other small pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and split open, while leaves begin to yellow and the plant starts to die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving only dried stems and empty seed capsules that may persist into winter.

funFact: Common figwort flowers are specifically designed for wasps, not bees - their dark reddish-brown color and slightly putrid smell mimic rotting meat to attract wasp pollinators, making this plant a 'wasp flower' in a world dominated by bee-pollinated plants.
confusionNotes: The square stem and opposite leaves might make you think of mints, but figwort lacks the aromatic smell and has those distinctive helmet-shaped brown flowers instead of the typical mint flower clusters. Remember: square stem + stinky smell + brown helmet flowers = figwort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'figwort,' this plant has nothing to do with fig trees - the name comes entirely from old medicinal beliefs about treating fig-shaped growths. It's actually more closely related to snapdragons and foxgloves than to any fig.
compareHints: Common figwort can be distinguished from late figwort by its more northern range and slightly smaller flowers, while lanceleaf figwort has much narrower, lance-shaped leaves rather than the broad, oval leaves of common figwort. All three species share the same distinctive helmet-shaped flowers and square stems, but leaf shape is the easiest way to tell them apart.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Late figwort blooms later than common figwort and grows taller, often reaching 8-10 feet versus common figwort's more modest 3-5 feet.
Lanceleaf figwort differs from common figwort by having narrower, more lance-shaped leaves (rather than broadly oval ones) and generally growing taller and more slender.
